catalog_quote: 13. STRESS. ... But stress can also be a phoneme, or significant and meaningful sound, in the Akianon dialect, since it strongly, influences meaning. ... The operation of stress in Akianon can be seen in two distinct ways. The first way shows stress to differentiate words that have no relationship at all in their meaning, so that Mispronunciation (that is, misplacing of stress) carries with it a very different meaning. Look at the following minimal pairs: MINIMAL PAIRS ILLUSTRATING STRESS DIFFERENCES & UNRELATED MEANING ... /tuba/ ("sugar- cane") /ttlbo/ ("pipe, tube") The fact that stress is phonemic it these cases should be obvious. Misplacement of stress in these cases makes it difficult (if not impossible) to convey the proper meaning. sources.citation: Zorc, R. David. 2005. Aklanon tag- and extra-systemic linguistic phenomena. In Hsiu-chuan Liao & Carl R. Galvez Rubino (eds.), Current Issues in Philippine Linguistics and Anthropology: Parangal kay Lawrence A. Reid, 124-135. Manila: LSP and SIL.
sources.quote: 'Unlike most verbal forms, which preserve the original accent pattern of the root, tag- may alternatively have a word-final effect on the accent pattern of any derivation with an open penult ... According to the phonotactic rules of Aklanon (and other Bisayan dialects), if the penult has a closed syllable, the accent always falls on the penult (Zorc 1977:243f). Hence no other accent pattern is possible.' Examples transcribe contrastive open-penult length vs final accent (tá:ngis 'cry' vs halín 'leave').

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David. 1995. Aklanon. In Darrell T. Tryon (ed.), Comparative Austronesian Dictionary, Part 1 Fascicle 1, 343-349. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. DOI 10.1515/9783110884012.1.343 (author-hosted scan, zorc.net item 093a).
sources.quote: 'Vowel length is phonemic and therefore differentiates root words: bá:ga? "lungs" ~ bagá? "swollen", há:pun "afternoon" ~ hapún "Japan(ese)" ... Stress is a feature of penultimate vowel length (vs shortness) and of syllable shape. Long vowels can only occur in an open penult. If the penult vowel is long, that syllable is accented, e.g. [ˈtu:bo] "pipe, tube". If the penultimate syllable is open and short, accent falls on the ultima, e.g. [tuˈboh] "sugarcane". If the penult consists of a closed syllable, i.e. CVC, accent falls on the penult, e.g. [ˈtuktuk].' Also p.343: 'The dialect reported her

sources.quote: Aklanon listed among Philippine languages with 'contrastive word accent': [lá:la] 'hurt' vs [lalá] 'braid'; 'In Philippine languages, vowel length (or shortness) is the most important feature of word accent'; 'Stress ... usually has a low functional load in words with a closed penult (CVC.CV(C)) ... Bisayan usually has CV́C.CV(C)'.

sources.quote: p.47: all Bs dialects share 'distinctive vowel length'; p.50: 'The vowel in an accented open penult (CV) is long ... In all dialects studied (except Kuy) stems or derivatives with a closed penult are accented on the penult (see 10.2.1)'; Akl is one of the two exemplifying dialects ('the dialect best known by me', p.62); p.243: 'all Bs dialects have penultimate rather than ultimate stress on inherited words with a closed penult'.

sources.quote: 'Aklanon spelling rarely, if ever, accounts for stress. Since stress is most important in distinguishing the meaning of words, the authors have endeavored to indicate stress as often as possible with the acute accent. Certain stress pairs will show the importance of such a symbol: túbo "pipe, tube" ~ tubó "sugar cane", píto ~ pitó ...'; p.42: unmarked words 'can be understood to be accented on the penultimate'.
